articles.title: Workday expands AI ambitions with C1.ai identity platform acquisition
articles.description: Fresh off its $1.1 billion acquisition of AI startup Sana, Workday is making another bet on enterprise AI, this time targeting the governance challenge. The company said it will acquire agentic identity platform C1.ai to help customers manage and secure AI agents operating across enterprise applications. The acquisition will build on Workday’s Agent System of Record, which gives enterprises a centralized view of their AI agents, by adding controls over what those agents can access across Workday and other enterprise systems, the company said. That would allow enterprises to grant agents the permissions they need to perform specific tasks and revoke them when those tasks are completed, rather than risk agents retaining access to data and applications they no longer need, it added. The combined capabilities could also help streamline access management for employees as they join an organization, change roles, or leave, reducing the manual work involved in managing permissions while limiting potential security gaps, it further said. These governance and identity management capabilities become increasingly important as Workday, alongside the acquisition, also continues to expand the role of AI agents across its suite. During the week, the company announced several updates to Sana, including making it the new home interface for its applications. The interface brings tasks, decisions, meetings, and agent activity into one place, allowing employees to use natural-language prompts to get Workday agents to complete tasks rather than simply retrieve information, the company said. The company also extended Sana into third-party tools, including Microsoft Teams, Slack, and Microsoft Copilot, allowing employees to invoke Workday capabilities from the applications they already use. That expanded ability to invoke Workday agents across applications underscores the need for enterprises to govern what these agents can access and do across systems. C1.ai’s acquisition is expected to close by the end of January.

articles.title: Ever wanted to train your own AI? This free Google tool makes it easy
articles.description: Sure, we all use AI in our everyday lives now, but what about taking a crack at training your own? Google Labs has a really cool project called Teachable Machine, which allows you to create and train your own basic AI model. The best part? You don’t need to know a thing about coding to do it. Right now it’s limited to making models that recognize images, sounds, and body poses. More capabilities may arrive in the future. Teach it the difference between a ripe banana and a green one, how to recognize a clap instead of a whistle, or even to tell whether you’re sitting or standing. Those are just ideas off the top of my head. You can let your imagination run wild. On the Teachable Machine website, click Get Started and choose whether you want to work with images, audio, or poses. Now it’s time to train the model by giving it examples to learn from. So, for example, if you’re training it to recognize images, you can upload photos or just use your webcam to show it different objects—the more examples the better. It’ll ask you to give each group of examples a name. Now click Train Model and watch it get to work. Once training is complete, you can show it new photos or use your webcam to see how well it recognizes different objects in real time. If it isn’t getting things right, then it’s time to get back to training. Add more examples, train it again, and see if it improves. It’s a great way to get a feel for why the data you feed an AI model is so important. If you want to take things a step further, you can even export your trained model and use it in your own website or app, although you’ll probably need some coding know-how for that. Otherwise, Teachable Machine is a fascinating afternoon project and an easy way to dip your toes into AI development.
